newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia top minister promises more cabinet changes.
newsitem.headline: Russia top minister promises more cabinet changes.

text.p: First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais has promised more surprise appointments in the course of Russia's most radical government reshuffle in five years.

The new-look cabinet, shaped by President Boris Yeltsin this week, meanwhile won its first prize on Tuesday-- a promise from combative trade unions not to demand its resignation during nationwide protest actions planned for March 27.

Chubais, Yeltsin's former chief of staff sent to the government as first deputy prime minister, said on Tuesday the reshuffle, which had washed out most conservative vice-premiers and replaced them with reformers, was not over.
"It is too early to put a final stop," Chubais told commercial NTV televison on Tuesday. "Some unexpected and important things may still happen. There will be more surprises."
Yeltsin, angered by failures to end chronic delays in wages and pensions, ordered Chernomyrdin to reshape the government and improve its performance in his state of the nation address on March 6.
The shuffle launched on Monday and intended, at least in part, to re-establish the president's authority after long illness reinforced the cabinet with senior reform-minded members.

Chernomyrdin is now backed by two first deputies -- Chubais, 41, who had spearheaded Russia's privatisation campaign, and Boris Nemtsov, 37, former reformist mayor of Nizhny Novgorod region. But some ministerial portfolios are still to be decided.
Chernomyrdin said that the government would focus on broadening and speeding up the reforms in the social and economic spheres.
"The situation in the country has to be quickly changed to the better and all conditions for it have been created," he said.
Trade unions, which have strongly criticised the government, appear to have softened their position after the latest changes.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted Labour Minister Alexander Melikyan as saying that during Tuesday's talks between Chernomyrdin and trade unions the latter promised not to demand the government's resignation on March 27.
"Such demands may only be moved in those regions where the unions do not control the situation," Melikyan said.
Union leaders could not be immediately reached for comment.
Chubais said he believed the cabinet could end the delays in wages and pensions but not immediately.

"It is impossible to solve the problem in a month or two," Chubais told NTV commercial television. "But I believe that if we act intensively we will be able to reach a visible breakthrough in six or eight months."
Interfax news agency said Chubais would take part in a trade union conference in the coal region of Kemerovo, where many anti-government protests have started in the past.
